**Part of:** [Chemistry](../index.qmd)

## Background

A chemical reaction is usually written as a reaction equation, e.g.,
$$ A \to B$$ {#eq-simple-reaction}

This simple reaction equation says that reactant (chemical) $A$ reacts to create
the product $B$. Some real chemical reaction equation examples follow.

## Examples {#sec-examples}

### Example 1: Hydrogen Peroxide Breakdown {#sec-hydrogen-peroxide-breakdown}
Hydrogen peroxide, $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$, slowly decomposes into water and oxygen
gas. This reaction is sped up by blood, causing bubbling, and sunlight, which is
why it's sold in brown containers. The reaction equation is
$$2\,\mathrm{H_2O_2} \to 2\,\mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{O_2}$$ {#eq-hydrogen-peroxide-breakdown}

This reaction equation says that $2$ hydrogen peroxide molecules break down to produce two molecules of water ($\mathrm{H_2O}$) and one molecule of oxygen gas ($\mathrm{O_2}$).

### Example 2: Bleaching with hydrogen peroxide[^bleaching] {#sec-hydrogen-peroxide-bleaching}
Hydrogen peroxide is used for bleaching paper and as a bleaching-agent in
laundry detergent. Borax ($\mathrm{Na_2 B_4 O_7}$), hydrogen peroxide
($\mathrm{H_2O_2}$), and Lye ($\mathrm{NaOH}$) combine to form sodium perborate
($\mathrm{Na_2 B_2 O_4 (OH)_4}$), a mild bleach. The reaction equation is
below.
 $$\mathrm{Na_2 B_4 O_7} + 4\mathrm{H_2O_2} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} \to 2
\mathrm{Na_2B_2O_4(OH)_4} + \mathrm{H_2O}$$

### Example 3: Hydrogen peroxide catalase {#sec-hydrogen-peroxide-catalase}
